title: The Lamb of God (John 1:19–34)
hookLine: John the Baptist points away from himself: behold the Lamb

lines: NOT THE CHRIST, NOT ELIJAH, NOT THE PROPHET.
cards: A delegation has walked out from Jerusalem to the river, priests and Levites, with one job: find out who this man is.
People are talking about John the Baptist, and every question they bring is a chance for him to make himself bigger. Who are you? Are you the Christ?
Are you that prophet? No. Then who?

teach.b: His answer, in the King James words: "I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, Make straight the way of the Lord, as said the prophet Esaias." Not a name.
A voice: something that exists to carry a message, then fades.

teach.h: NOT WORTHY TO UNDO HIS SANDAL.
teach.b: About the one coming after him, he says he isn't worthy to undo his sandal strap, a servant's job.
The next day, he sees Jesus walking toward him, and he points: "Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world." Readers have heard more than one lamb in that title.

The Passover lamb, whose blood marked the doors in Egypt on the night of freedom. The lambs offered morning and evening at the altar, in the book of Exodus. And the servant in Isaiah, brought as a lamb to the slaughter.
Readers differ on which one John the Baptist meant; the Gospel may want all of them. Later in this Gospel, Jesus is condemned on the day John calls the preparation of the Passover.

teach.h: THE SPIRIT LIKE A DOVE, REMAINING.
teach.b: Then John tells what he saw at the river: the Spirit coming down from heaven like a dove, and staying on him. He didn't know who it would be until he saw that.
I saw, he says, and I bear witness that this is the Son of God. Notice what John the Baptist does with all his fame. He uses it to point.
Behold. That's the one. And the very next day, two of his own disciples will follow his finger and leave him.

how: In the Catholic Mass, and in Lutheran and Anglican communion services that keep it, the congregation sings or says the Agnus Dei, a short chant built on John the Baptist's words, Lamb of God, before receiving the bread and wine.

o: a lamb, the young sheep John points Jesus out as
a shepherd who guards and leads the flock
a ram offered in place of a son on an altar

games.q: what's inside John 1:19–34 — tap the pairs.
p: not worthy to undo it, John says

s: John the Baptist says he is Elijah come back
asked if he is Elijah, he says, I am not. he calls himself a voice.
the title 'Lamb of God' calls up more than one lamb
readers hear the Passover lamb, the daily lambs of Exodus 29, and Isaiah's lamb.
John says he recognized Jesus by the Spirit coming down like a dove
he says, I knew him not, until he saw the Spirit descend and remain on him.

games.q: you're John the Baptist. crowds follow you; leaders want to know if you're the Christ. Jesus walks toward you. what do you do?
o: point at him: behold the Lamb of God.
keep quiet and let people decide.
games.why: "behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world." he spends his fame pointing away from himself.

practice: Think of someone whose good work goes unnoticed: a teammate who fixed the problem you got credit for, a quietly kind friend, a nurse, a neighbor.
Picture pointing to them out loud, the way John pointed, behold, look at what this person did; it doesn't make you smaller, it makes you a voice. If you pray, you can give thanks for them.

wordCard.voice: Amnos, the Greek word for a young sheep, a lamb: John the Baptist's name for Jesus as he pointed him out, the one who takes away the sin of the world.

orig.note: Greek: the Lamb of God. amnos is the word for a young sheep, used in Isaiah 53:7 in the Greek Old Testament.

carryVoice: Your line: behold the lamb. A voice, not a name, pointing away from itself. That's five hundred ninety-four.
